title: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle
openingChapterLabel: Book I — The Good for Man
openingText: Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims, it is thought, at some good: for which reason a common and by no means a bad description of the Chief Good is, "that which all things aim at." Now there plainly is a difference in the Ends proposed: for in some cases they are acts of working, and in others certain works or tangible results beyond and beside the acts of working: and where there are certain Ends beyond and beside the actions, the works are in their nature better than the acts of working.
about:
The Nicomachean Ethics is Aristotle's treatise on how to live well. It asks what the human good is, how virtues are identified and developed, what role pleasure and friendship play in a flourishing life, and how the intellectual virtues relate to the moral ones. The book is built around the concept of eudaimonia — usually translated as happiness or flourishing — and the claim that flourishing is not a feeling but an activity, the lifelong exercise of distinctively human capacities in accordance with virtue. Aristotle works systematically through the major virtues — courage, generosity, magnanimity, justice, temperance — and devotes three of the ten books to friendship.

Aristotle composed the Ethics in Athens in the 330s and 320s BCE, during his second period at the Lyceum. The text we have is almost certainly his lecture notes, possibly compiled or edited by his son Nicomachus, after whom it is named. It is divided into ten books. Books I–II establish the framework — eudaimonia, the doctrine of the mean, virtue as habituation. Books III–V treat the moral virtues. Book VI handles the intellectual virtues. Book VII treats weakness of will and pleasure. Books VIII–IX are on friendship. Book X returns to happiness and concludes with the claim that the highest life is one of philosophical contemplation.

It is the founding work of Western virtue ethics — the tradition that asks what kind of person to become rather than what kind of action to perform. Aristotle's framework — virtue as habituated disposition rather than rule-following, practical wisdom as the master capacity, the doctrine of the mean as the structure of moral excellence — shaped Christian ethics through Aquinas, fell out of fashion in the early modern period as Kant and the utilitarians took the field, and has been substantially revived since the middle of the twentieth century by writers including Elizabeth Anscombe, Alasdair MacIntyre, and Martha Nussbaum.

angleCards.title: Flourishing, not happiness.
angleCards.text: The word we translate as happiness — eudaimonia — does not mean a feeling. It means a life fully lived, in the exercise of distinctively human capacities. Aristotle's answer to "what should I want?" is more demanding and more interesting than modern self-help's version of the same question.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand eudaimonia as Aristotle meant it — not subjective happiness but the objective activity of living well — and see what that demands of a person across a lifetime.

angleCards.title: The mean between excess and deficiency.
angleCards.text: Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between miserliness and profligacy. For every virtue, Aristotle identifies two corresponding failures. The doctrine of the mean is not a call to mediocrity — it is a call to precision: hitting the right response, at the right time, toward the right person.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the doctrine of the mean through Aristotle's catalogue of virtues — and ask whether this framework actually tracks the moral reality of specific virtues or whether it strains under the weight of some of them.

angleCards.title: Friendship as the heart of a good life.
angleCards.text: Three books out of ten are on friendship. Aristotle believes no one would choose to live without friends, even with every other good. He distinguishes friendships of utility, pleasure, and virtue — and argues that the third kind, built on mutual admiration of character, is both rare and constitutive of who we become.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Nicomachean Ethics primarily through its treatment of friendship — what Aristotle thinks genuine friendship requires, why he gives it so much weight, and whether his three-tier distinction holds up.

angleCards.title: Practical wisdom as the master virtue.
angleCards.text: Phronesis — practical wisdom — is the capacity to see what a situation calls for and respond accordingly. It cannot be taught by rule. It is developed through experience, and it governs every other virtue. Aristotle argues that knowing ethics theoretically is nearly useless. The goal is to become a person who perceives and acts rightly.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the role of phronesis across the Ethics — how Aristotle distinguishes practical from theoretical knowledge, and what it means that good character cannot be reduced to following principles.

cast.name: Eudaimonia
cast.description: The end toward which all human action ultimately aims. Not a feeling of happiness but an activity — the ongoing exercise of one's distinctively human capacities in accordance with virtue. Aristotle argues you cannot have it for a moment, and you cannot know whether someone has had it until their life is complete. It requires not just good character but external goods — friends, modest wealth, decent fortune — because human flourishing is not invulnerable to circumstance. The whole Ethics is the unpacking of this one term.

cast.name: The Golden Mean
cast.description: Every moral virtue is the midpoint between two vices: excess on one side, deficiency on the other. Courage stands between recklessness and cowardice. Generosity between profligacy and miserliness. Truthfulness between boastfulness and false modesty. The mean is not a fixed point on a number line; it varies by person, situation, and context, and finding it requires perception rather than calculation. The doctrine has shaped the way virtues have been described in the West for two and a half thousand years.

cast.name: Practical Wisdom (Phronesis)
cast.description: The intellectual virtue that governs all the moral ones. Phronesis is the ability to perceive what a particular situation morally requires and to act accordingly — not by applying a principle to the case but by seeing the case clearly. Aristotle argues it cannot be taught directly; it grows through experience and the habituation of good action. Without it, the moral virtues do not function. Iris Murdoch and Alasdair MacIntyre rebuilt much of modern virtue ethics around this concept.

cast.name: Friendship (Philia)
cast.description: Aristotle devotes three of ten books to friendship — Books VIII and IX and the back end of VII — which tells you how seriously he takes it. He distinguishes three kinds: friendships of utility, of pleasure, and of virtue. Only the third is friendship in the full sense — built on mutual recognition of each other's character. It is rare, he says, takes time to form, and is the form in which each friend is constitutive of the other's good life.

cast.name: Virtue (Arete)
cast.description: Not an act but a disposition — a stable, habituated tendency to feel, perceive, and respond in the right way. Virtues are acquired through practice: you become courageous by doing courageous things until courage feels natural rather than effortful. Once formed, they shape what you notice, what you want, and what you find pleasant. The goal is not to control yourself against your inclinations but to become someone whose inclinations are themselves rightly ordered. Aristotle is unsentimental about how long this takes.

cast.name: Contemplation (Theoria)
cast.description: In Book X, Aristotle argues that the best human life is one devoted to philosophical contemplation — the activity that is most self-sufficient, most continuous, most purely its own end, and most like the activity of the divine. This appears to contradict everything in the previous nine books about virtuous civic life. The tension is real, and readers have argued ever since about whether it is a contradiction, a hierarchy, or two compatible accounts of flourishing.

whyItMatters.title: A Theory of Happiness That Is Not About Feelings
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle's eudaimonia is not a state of mood but a quality of activity over a complete life. The argument is that you cannot tell whether a person has flourished from how they feel at any given moment — flourishing is a feature of how the whole life goes, and you cannot know it until the life is over. Aristotle was prepared to say that a virtuous person who suffered great misfortune would not be flourishing, and that this was not a flaw in the theory but a feature of human life. The argument is a direct rebuke to most modern psychological theories of well-being, which measure happiness in self-reported subjective states. Martin Seligman's positive psychology has tried to recover something of the older view.

whyItMatters.title: Virtue as Habit, Not Rule
whyItMatters.body: For Aristotle, becoming a good person is not about learning the right principles but about developing the right habits — practicing courage until courage feels natural, practicing generosity until generosity is what you want to do. The model has shaped most serious thinking about character in the West, from Aquinas through to the modern revival of virtue ethics in Anscombe, Foot, and MacIntyre. It is also the philosophical root of the contemporary observation that what we repeatedly do is what we become — the framing James Clear and Stephen Covey both work from, several layers downstream from the original. Aristotle is the source. Knowing the source changes how the claim reads.

whyItMatters.title: The Mean Between Extremes
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle argues that most virtues are means between two excesses — courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and waste, truthfulness between boasting and self-deprecation. The doctrine sounds simple and is not. The mean is not a midpoint in any mechanical sense; it is the response that fits the situation, and locating it requires the practical wisdom Aristotle treats as the master capacity. The doctrine has shaped the moral vocabulary of the West for twenty-four centuries — every list of virtues from Cicero through Aquinas through C. S. Lewis is structured around a version of it. It has its critics; even Aristotle has trouble forcing some virtues, like justice, into the framework.
